prompt: What does `--top-k 2` do to the list of next words?
hint: Read the table for `the coffee is` with k = 2.

choices.text: Keeps the two best and rescales them to 100%
choices.why: Right. `hot` and `strong` survive, and their shares become 76.2% and 23.8%.

choices.text: Halves every share
choices.why: Nothing is halved. Three words are removed and two are scaled up.

choices.text: Keeps every word but squeezes the tail, the way a low temperature does
choices.why: That is temperature's job. Top-k removes words outright.

choices.text: Draws twice and keeps the more common of the two words
choices.why: Top-k does not draw. It cuts the list, and one draw follows.

prompt: After `the coffee is`, `hot` has 59.3% and `strong` 18.5%. With `--top-k 2`, what share does `hot` get, in percent?
hint: Divide 59.3 by the two shares added together.

prompt: Scaling the surviving shares back up so they add up to 100% is called ___.
hint: The word in the first paragraph after the table.
How many words can be drawn?

choices.text: Temperature 1 with no other controls set on the request
choices.why: That keeps every word the model scored.

choices.text: Temperature 0
choices.why: Right. One word survives, so the top word is taken every time: greedy decoding.

choices.text: Top-p of 1
choices.why: A top-p of 1 keeps everything.

choices.text: A draw of one sample
choices.why: `--samples` sets how many continuations are written, not how many words are kept.

prompt: With `--top-k 2` after `the`, `coffee` and `café` are kept. Why is that a problem for k = 2 here?
hint: Add up what was thrown away.

choices.text: It keeps too many words, because only one was ever likely
choices.why: Eight candidates, none above 30%: the model was torn, not sure.

choices.text: It throws away more than half of what the model considered likely
choices.why: Right: 48.1% is kept, and `bread`, `cat` and `tea` were plausible. The same k that suits `the coffee is` is far too tight here.

choices.text: Top-k cannot be used at the start of a sentence
choices.why: It can be used anywhere. It just keeps a count that ignores the shape of the list.

choices.text: `café` should have been dropped for its accent
choices.why: Characters play no part. It was kept for having the second-highest share.

hint: Read the definition at the top of the section.

choices.text: The smallest set of top words whose shares reach p
choices.why: Right. Words are added from the top until the running total reaches p.

choices.text: Every word whose own share, taken alone, is above p
choices.why: With p = 0.8, that would keep nothing after `the coffee is`, where no word has 80%.

choices.text: The top p words
choices.why: That is top-k, a count. Top-p is a share.

choices.text: A share p of every word's probability
choices.why: Shares are not reduced one by one; whole words are dropped.

prompt: How many words did `toylm dist "and the" --top-p 0.8` keep?
hint: Count the lines of the table.

prompt: With p = 0.8, why is only the full stop kept after `the coffee is hot`?

choices.text: Top-p always keeps exactly one word
choices.why: After `and the` it kept four.

choices.text: `and` scored below the 20% minimum that top-p requires
choices.why: There is no per-word minimum. `and` went because the total was reached before it.

choices.text: Its 85% share on its own already passes 0.8, so the count stops
choices.why: Right. The running total reached p with the first word, so nothing more was added.

choices.text: The model was told the sentence had ended
choices.why: Nobody told it anything. The full stop was simply most likely after `is hot`.

prompt: `café` and `terrace` both had 11.8% after `and the`, and top-p 0.8 kept `café`. Why `café`?
hint: The same rule decided a tie at temperature 0.

choices.text: Its share was higher, if you read the hidden decimals
choices.why: The counts are equal: two each. There are no hidden decimals.

choices.text: Top-p prefers shorter words
choices.why: Length plays no part.

choices.text: Ties sort alphabetically
choices.why: Right. `toylm` orders tied words alphabetically, so `café` comes first and the total passes 0.8 with it.

choices.text: A random draw broke the tie
choices.why: Nothing is drawn while the nucleus is formed.

prompt: Why is top-p said to adapt where top-k does not?
hint: Compare `is hot` and `and the` under both controls.

choices.text: It learns the right value of p from the outputs it has produced before
choices.why: Nothing is learnt. The same p acts on a different list in each place.

choices.text: It keeps few words when the model is sure and more when it is torn
choices.why: Right: one word after `is hot`, four after `and the`, from the same p. Top-k kept two in both places.

choices.text: It is applied before temperature, so it sees the raw scores
choices.why: In `toylm` it runs after temperature, and that is why temperature changes it.

choices.text: It removes only the words that are wrong
choices.why: It removes unlikely words. A kept word can still be wrong for your purpose.

prompt: With top-p 0.8 set, you raise the temperature from 1 to 2. How many words survive after `the coffee is`?

choices.text: More: four instead of three
choices.why: Right. Flattened shares need more words to reach 80%.

choices.text: The same three, since top-p is independent
choices.why: They act on the same list in sequence, so they are not independent.

choices.text: Fewer: two instead of three
choices.why: That is what lowering the temperature tends to do.

choices.text: All five
choices.why: Four reach 80%; `bitter` is still cut.

prompt: Put the controls in the order `toylm` applies them.
hint: The docstring at the top of the program.

prompt: You changed temperature and top-p in one go, and the output improved. What can you conclude?

choices.text: Both changes helped equally
choices.why: Nothing in a single comparison says that.

choices.text: Top-p helped, since temperature only adds randomness
choices.why: Temperature also widens or narrows the nucleus that top-p keeps.

choices.text: Temperature helped, since top-p has no effect when temperature is set
choices.why: Top-p changed the result at every temperature shown.

choices.text: You cannot tell which change did it
choices.why: Right. They act on the same list and affect each other, so a joint change hides which one mattered. Change one at a time.

prompt: Top-k 3 and top-p 0.8 are both set after `the coffee is`. What survives in `toylm`?
hint: Each one removes words; which set is smaller?

choices.text: `hot` and `strong`
choices.why: That would need k = 2.

choices.text: All five words
choices.why: Both controls cut `cold` and `bitter`.

choices.text: `hot`, `strong` and `ready`
choices.why: Right. Both controls keep those three, so the smaller set is the same set.

choices.text: Only `hot`
choices.why: That happened at temperature 0.5 with top-p 0.8, not here.

prompt: You want to use top-k on an API, and its reference never mentions a top-k parameter. What should you assume?
hint: What does the section say about the set of controls?

choices.text: It is there under the same name, undocumented
choices.why: Do not assume a parameter exists because another provider has it.

choices.text: Take it that the API does not offer top-k at all
choices.why: Right. The controls are each provider's choice; some well-known APIs have no top-k.

choices.text: Top-p is the same thing under another name
choices.why: Top-p is a share and top-k a count; they behave differently.

choices.text: Sending it anyway is harmless
choices.why: An API may reject it, or quietly ignore it and leave you believing it worked.

prompt: Which of these does this lesson recommend? Choose all that apply.
hint: One section is called "One control at a time".

choices.text: Adjust temperature first, leaving top-k and top-p at their defaults
choices.why: Yes. It has the most visible, continuous effect.

choices.text: Reach for top-p when output occasionally goes strange
choices.why: Yes. It trims the tail without flattening the common choices.

choices.text: Change two controls together to save time
choices.why: Then you cannot tell which one did what.

choices.text: Follow the provider's advice where it says not to tune temperature and top-p together
choices.why: Yes. Some providers recommend changing one or the other.

prompt: Match each setting to what it kept after `the coffee is` in `toylm`.
A model at your preferred temperature writes well, but now and then a reply veers into an odd word. Which single change does this lesson point to?
hint: Which control removes the tail without reshaping the rest?

choices.text: Lower the temperature to 0 so nothing is drawn
choices.why: That removes all variety, which you said you liked.

choices.text: Set top-k to 1
choices.why: Same as temperature 0: it removes all the variety you wanted to keep.

choices.text: Raise the temperature so odd words become more usual
choices.why: That makes them more frequent, not less.

choices.text: Set top-p a little below 1
choices.why: Right. It cuts the unlikely tail in each context and leaves the confident choices as they were.
